title: Web Crawler
prompt: Design a crawler that downloads billions of web pages for a search index and keeps them reasonably fresh, without hammering any website or getting stuck in endless link mazes.

clarify.q: How many pages, and how often must each be refreshed?
clarify.why: Pages per second and bandwidth come straight from this. A monthly refresh of 5 B pages is about 2 k pages/s; a daily refresh would be 30× that.

clarify.q: HTML only, or also images, PDFs and JavaScript-rendered pages?
clarify.why: Rendering JavaScript needs a headless browser per page, roughly 10 to 100 times the CPU of parsing HTML. It is usually a separate, smaller pipeline for pages that need it.

clarify.q: Who consumes the output: a search indexer, an ML dataset, an archive?
clarify.why: An indexer wants fresh pages and change notifications. An archive wants every version kept. That decides storage layout and retention.

clarify.q: What politeness rules do we commit to?
clarify.why: Obeying robots.txt, crawl-delay and a per-host rate cap is the price of not being blocked. Per-host limits are the hardest constraint on throughput, not our bandwidth.

clarify.q: Should near-duplicate pages (mirrors, printer views) be stored once?
clarify.why: A large share of the web is copies. Detecting near-duplicates saves storage and keeps the index clean but needs fingerprinting, not just exact hashes.

clarify.q: Do we start from a seed list, and which parts of the web matter most?
clarify.why: Priority decides which URLs get the limited per-host budget first: a news home page should beat page 900 of a forum archive.

functional: Start from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, and keep discovering new URLs.
Obey robots.txt and never exceed a per-host request rate.
Fetch each canonical URL at most once per refresh cycle; store each distinct content once.
Recrawl pages on a schedule based on how often they change and how important they are.
Detect and escape crawler traps (infinite calendars, session-id loops, generated pages).
Store raw content and metadata for downstream indexing.
nonFunctional: Throughput: 5 B pages per 30-day cycle, about 2 k pages/s sustained.
Politeness: by default at most 1 request per second per host, lower when the site is slow or asks.
Fault tolerant: a crawler node dying loses at most a few minutes of in-flight work, not its frontier.
Horizontally scalable by adding fetch nodes.
Extensible: new content types and parsers can be plugged in.
outOfScope: Building the search index and ranking.
Logging in to sites or crawling behind paywalls.
Full JavaScript rendering for every page (a separate small lane).

assumptions: Average HTML page 100 KB uncompressed; stored compressed about 4:1
About 50 B distinct URLs discovered over time (10 per fetched page)
Average fetch takes about 1 s including connection setup

steps.label: Bandwidth
steps.result: ≈ 1.6 Gbit/s inbound: a handful of well-connected machines

steps.label: Storage per cycle
steps.math: 5 B × 100 KB = 500 TB raw; ÷ 4 compression = 125 TB
steps.result: ≈ 125 TB per cycle in object storage

steps.label: Seen-URL Bloom filter
steps.math: 1% false positives needs ~9.6 bits per URL; 50 B × 9.6 bits = 480 Gbit = 60 GB
steps.result: ≈ 60 GB, split across nodes by host

steps.label: Concurrent fetches
steps.math: Little's law: 2 000/s × 1 s = 2 000 in flight; slow tail at 3 s → 6 000
steps.result: ≈ 6 k open connections: async I/O on tens of nodes

steps.label: Ceiling for one big host
steps.result: A 100 M page site cannot be fully refreshed monthly: prioritise within hosts

estimates.takeaway: Raw throughput is modest: 2 k pages/s and 1.6 Gbit/s. The hard limits are per host: at 1 request/s one site gives us at most 2.6 M pages a month, so the frontier must spread work across millions of hosts and pick the best pages within each. Dedupe state is large (60 GB of Bloom filter for URLs alone), so it is partitioned along with the frontier by host.

api.note: Routed to the node owning each URL's host; that node drops already-seen URLs.
Only returns a URL whose host is ready under its rate limit.

api.body: { url, status, contentHash, simhash, storageKey, fetchedAt, changed }
api.note: Indexer skips pages where changed is false.
Manual overrides when a site owner complains or a trap is found.

entities.name: UrlRecord
entities.store: RocksDB on the owning crawler node (plus backup to object storage)
entities.why: Exact record per known URL. The Bloom filter in front avoids most disk lookups for new URLs.

entities.name: HostState
entities.store: In memory on the owning node, checkpointed
entities.why: Politeness and trap budgets are per host, so the host is the unit of ownership.

entities.name: Document
entities.store: Object storage, keyed by contentHash, compressed
entities.why: Content-addressed: the same bytes served by 20 mirror URLs are stored once.

entities.name: Fingerprint
entities.why: Finds near-duplicates (same article, different ads) by small bit distance.

data.note: Everything about a URL lives on the node that owns its host, chosen by consistent hashing on the host name. That keeps politeness, robots rules, the seen-set and the frontier for one host in one place with no cross-node locking. Content is stored by hash, so exact duplicates cost nothing extra.

hld.summary:
The crawl is a loop. A URL frontier decides what to fetch next while respecting per-host rate limits. Fetchers resolve DNS through a caching resolver, check the cached robots.txt, download with timeouts and size caps, and write the body to object storage keyed by content hash. A parser extracts links and text, computes content fingerprints, and emits page.fetched.

Extracted links are normalised, filtered (trap rules, file types, robots), and sent to the frontier partition that owns their host, which checks the seen-set (Bloom filter then exact store) and enqueues new ones with a priority. A recrawl scheduler puts known URLs back into the frontier when their nextFetchAt arrives.

diagram.title: Crawl loop
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  SEED[Seed URLs] --> FR[URL frontier per host partition]
  SCH[Recrawl scheduler] --> FR
  FR --> F[Fetchers, async HTTP]
  F --> DNS["DNS cache"]
  F --> RB["robots.txt cache"]
  F --> OS[("Object storage by content hash")]
  F --> P[Parser and link extractor]
  P --> CD["Content dedupe (hash and SimHash)"]
  P --> UF[URL normaliser and trap filter]
  UF --> SEEN[("Seen-set: Bloom + RocksDB")]
  SEEN --> FR
  CD --> IDX[["page.fetched to indexer"]]

flows.title: Fetching one page
steps: Frontier hands a fetcher example.com/news, whose host's nextAllowedAt has passed, and sets nextAllowedAt to now plus the crawl delay.
Fetcher resolves DNS from cache, confirms robots.txt allows the path, GETs with a 30 s timeout and a 10 MB cap.
Body is hashed; if the hash equals the last fetch, record 'unchanged' and stop.
Otherwise store it compressed by content hash, parse links, compute SimHash, emit page.fetched.

flows.title: Handling a discovered link
steps: Normalise: lowercase host, drop the fragment, sort query parameters, strip known session and tracking parameters.
Apply filters: URL length, path repetition, depth from seed, file type, host page budget.
Route by host hash to the owning node; check the Bloom filter; if 'maybe seen', confirm in RocksDB.
New URL: insert UrlRecord and enqueue with priority from link source and page signals.

flows.title: Recrawling a known page
steps: Scheduler finds URLs whose nextFetchAt has passed and adds them to the frontier at their priority.
Fetch with If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match; a 304 costs almost nothing.
Update changeRate from whether content changed and set nextFetchAt sooner or later accordingly.

deepDives.title: URL frontier design
deepDives.problem: The frontier holds billions of URLs and must answer one question 2 000 times a second: what is the most important URL whose host we are allowed to hit right now? A plain FIFO queue fails both halves: it ignores importance, and long runs of URLs from one host either break politeness or block the queue while we wait.

options.name: One global FIFO queue (Kafka topic)
options.how: Discovered URLs are appended; fetchers consume in order.
cons: A site with 1 M links in a row stalls fetchers or gets hammered
No priority; no notion of 'host not ready yet'

options.name: Per-host queues with a ready-time heap
options.how: Each host has its own queue. A min-heap keyed by nextAllowedAt says which host is ready next. Fetchers pop the heap, take the host's best URL, and push the host back with its new ready time.
cons: Millions of host queues need to spill to disk
Priority across hosts is coarse

options.name: Priority front tiers feeding per-host back queues
options.how: New URLs enter one of a few priority tiers. A selector drains higher tiers more often into the per-host queues, which are served by the ready-time heap.
pros: Tiers are easy to reason about
cons: More moving parts
Starvation of low tiers needs weighted draining

deepDives.choice: Priority tiers feeding per-host queues with a ready-time heap, partitioned across crawler nodes by host so each node owns its hosts outright. Host queues keep the head in memory and the rest in RocksDB. With about 2 k fetches/s and most hosts allowed 1/s, the heap always has plenty of ready hosts. If we only crawled a fixed list of a few thousand large sites, a single per-host scheduler would be enough and tiers would add little.

diagram.title: Inside one frontier partition
diagram.src:
flowchart TD
  IN[New and due URLs] --> PRI[Prioritiser]
  PRI --> T1[High tier]
  PRI --> T2[Medium tier]
  PRI --> T3[Low tier]
  T1 --> SEL[Weighted selector]
  T2 --> SEL
  T3 --> SEL
  SEL --> HQ["Per-host queues (RAM head, RocksDB tail)"]
  HQ --> HEAP[Heap ordered by host nextAllowedAt]
  HEAP --> FET[Fetcher takes a ready host]
  FET --> HEAP

deepDives.title: Politeness and robots.txt
deepDives.problem: A crawler that ignores site owners gets blocked by IP and complained about. The rules come from several places: robots.txt allow and disallow lines, an optional crawl-delay, server signals like 429 and 503 with Retry-After, and the plain fact that many small sites share one IP address on cheap hosting.

options.name: Fixed delay per host
options.how: Wait a fixed 1 s between requests to the same host name.
cons: Too slow for big sites that can take more
Too fast for a tiny site on a shared server
Ignores hosts sharing one IP

options.name: Adaptive per-host rate with IP-level cap
options.how: Start at the robots crawl-delay or 1 s. Slow down when response time rises or on 429/503; speed up slowly for fast, healthy hosts up to a ceiling. Also cap requests per IP address across all hosts on it.
pros: Polite to weak servers, efficient on strong ones
cons: More state per host and per IP
IP cap needs DNS results to group hosts

deepDives.choice: Adaptive rate plus an IP cap. robots.txt is fetched per host and cached up to 24 h; if fetching it fails with 5xx we treat the host as fully disallowed until it succeeds, which is the safe reading. We send an honest user agent with a contact URL, follow Retry-After, and pause a host for an hour after repeated 5xx. A large site that wants faster crawling can be raised by an admin policy. If we crawled only partners who opted in, a fixed agreed rate would be fine.

deepDives.title: Dedupe: URLs with Bloom filters, content with hashes
deepDives.problem: Two different duplicate problems. URL dedupe: each page links to dozens of URLs we already know; checking 20 k+ discovered links a second against 50 B known URLs on disk is slow. Content dedupe: different URLs often serve the same or nearly the same page (mirrors, tracking parameters, printer versions), which wastes storage and pollutes the index.

options.name: Exact seen-set in a key-value store
options.how: Look up every normalised URL hash in RocksDB or a distributed KV store.
pros: Can store metadata with the key
cons: A disk read per discovered link, mostly for URLs we already know

options.name: Bloom filter in front of the exact store
options.how: Keep a per-partition Bloom filter in RAM. 'Definitely not seen' means new: insert without a disk read. 'Maybe seen' means check the exact store.
pros: New URLs skip the disk entirely
60 GB of RAM in total, split across nodes
cons: Cannot delete entries; rebuild periodically
Known URLs still need the disk check (but those are cached hot)

options.name: Content hash plus SimHash
options.how: Exact 128-bit hash of the normalised body catches identical copies. A 64-bit SimHash over shingles of the text catches near-copies within a few bits.
pros: Near-dupes are flagged for the indexer
cons: SimHash lookup by bit distance needs a block-split index
Threshold tuning: too loose merges different pages

deepDives.choice: Bloom filter in front of an exact store for URLs, so a Bloom false positive only costs a disk read and never makes us skip a new URL. Using the Bloom filter alone at 1% would silently drop about 1 in 100 new URLs, which some crawlers accept but I would not for a search index. For content, use an exact hash to store bodies once and SimHash with a 3-bit threshold to mark near-duplicates and pick one canonical URL. If RAM were tight, I would accept the Bloom-only approach for low-priority tiers.

deepDives.title: Crawler traps
deepDives.problem: Some sites generate unlimited URLs: a calendar with a 'next month' link forever, session ids added to every link, search pages for every word combination, or relative links that keep nesting paths like /a/b/a/b/a/b. A naive crawler spends its whole budget on one site and still never finishes.

options.name: Hard limits on URLs
options.how: Cap URL length (say 2 000 chars), path depth, and repeated path segments.
cons: Does not catch a calendar with short, clean URLs

options.name: Per-host page budget by importance
options.how: Each host gets a page budget per cycle that scales with its importance; once spent, the rest waits.
pros: Bounds the damage of any trap
cons: A big, legit site may be under-crawled until its importance is known

options.name: Pattern and yield detection
options.how: Track, per host and URL pattern (path with numbers replaced), how many new pages and how much new content it yields. Patterns producing many URLs with near-duplicate content get demoted.
pros: Catches traps the simple rules miss
cons: Needs tuning and occasional manual review
Can demote real paginated content

deepDives.choice: Use all three in layers: hard URL limits and parameter stripping at normalisation, a per-host budget, and yield detection that demotes patterns where most fetches are near-duplicates or soft 404s. An admin override per host fixes false positives. If we were crawling a curated list of known sites, budgets plus hard limits would be enough.

failures: Its host partitions move to other nodes via consistent hashing; they reload frontier and UrlRecords from the RocksDB checkpoint in object storage; in-flight URLs are refetched.
Local caching resolvers per node with TTL respect, prefetching for hosts about to become ready; a slow lookup does not block other fetches.
A site starts returning 503 to us
Exponential backoff on that host, honour Retry-After, pause after repeated failures, alert if a top host is affected.
Frontier grows faster than we can crawl
Low-priority tiers are trimmed; new URLs below a priority floor are recorded but not enqueued.
Parser crashes on a malformed page
Parse in sandboxed worker processes with memory and time limits; mark the URL and move on.
Bloom filter fills beyond its design size
False-positive rate climbs, which only costs extra disk reads; rebuild a larger filter from the exact store in the background.
scale: 10× pages (daily refresh of top pages plus monthly long tail): about 20 k fetches/s and 16 Gbit/s; add fetch nodes and partitions; politeness still limits each host, so prioritisation matters more than hardware.
Geography: run fetchers in several regions and assign hosts to the region closest to their servers to cut latency and cross-region traffic.
JavaScript-heavy sites: a separate render lane with headless browsers, fed only URLs whose HTML looks empty or app-shell-like, with its own strict budget.

followups.q: How do you decide when to recrawl a page?
answer: Estimate each page's change rate from past fetches (changed or not).
Set the next visit interval roughly inversely to change rate, weighted by importance, within min and max bounds.
Use conditional GETs so unchanged pages are cheap; sitemaps with lastmod help too.

followups.q: Why partition by host instead of by URL hash?
answer: Politeness, robots rules and trap budgets are per host; one owner means no distributed locks.
Downside: a giant host is one partition's job, but politeness caps its rate anyway.
Use the registered domain for grouping subdomains when needed.

followups.q: How do you handle redirects and canonical tags?
answer: Follow up to 5 redirects; record the final URL as canonical for the original.
Respect rel=canonical as a hint and merge duplicate records.
Count redirects against the host budget to stop redirect loops.

followups.q: How do you recover the whole crawl after a bug corrupts state?
answer: Frontier and UrlRecords are checkpointed per partition to object storage.
Documents are immutable and content-addressed, so they are safe.
Restore checkpoints and replay page.fetched events since then.

followups.q: How would you prioritise which new URLs to fetch?
answer: Signals: importance of linking pages, number of distinct linking hosts, depth from seed, host quality.
New hosts get a small trial budget.
Revisit priority uses change rate times importance.

mistakes: Using a single FIFO queue and adding politeness as an afterthought.
Using a Bloom filter alone and not noticing it silently skips new URLs on false positives.
Deduping only by URL, so mirrors and tracking-parameter variants are stored many times.
No trap defences, so one calendar page eats the crawl budget.
Spending the interview on the HTML parser instead of the frontier, politeness and dedupe.

senior: Designed the frontier with per-host queues and a ready-time scheduler, partitioned by host
Used a Bloom filter in front of an exact store and explained false positives
Separated URL dedupe from content dedupe and used hashes plus near-duplicate fingerprints
Gave at least three concrete trap defences
Computed the per-host ceiling and drew a conclusion about prioritisation
staff: Designed adaptive recrawl scheduling from estimated change rates with conditional GETs
Handled shared-IP hosting and adaptive slowdown on server signals
Planned checkpointing and partition handoff for node failure
Scoped JavaScript rendering as a separate budgeted lane
